blocks.cap: The membrane, drawn at last to its true scale

blocks.p: Thirty-one index cards covered the floor of Higuchi's back room at the Crooked Shelf, each one a favour the Healer had done in Gin's body, each one written out in Rei's cramped hand. Between them, in red pencil, ran the seams Kishin had scored through the city, the ones Kaito preached over in the drained pool. Rei knelt among them with the lamp pulled down low, moving a card a finger's width, then another. Around midnight he stopped seeing two patterns. Having the plan whole was worse than not having it had ever been. He saw one engine, and Kita-ku was the cylinder it fired in.

The membrane was not a wall, whatever he had let himself picture. It was not a thin bright sheet hung between the living city and the place the dead pass through when the lanterns call them home. It was a pressure. It was a breath the world had been holding since before the wards had names. And for a month the thing wearing his brother had been teaching the city, mercy by careful mercy, to let that breath out.

Every healing was a loosening. He understood it now, sick and certain, the way the body knows a thing before the mind allows it. A grieving man's haunting was closed gently, and the closing borrowed a little of the tension that held Kita's seam shut. A drowned client was laid to rest, and another fraction was spent. Thirty-one acts of kindness, every one of them seen and every one of them thanked, and each one drew the smallest possible thread from the one place in Tokyo where the wall was already a scar. Kita had been weakening since 2009, the year something in it went empty. March 2011 had torn it further. Now the held breath over that old wound was no longer a wall at all. It was a curtain, and a curtain is a thing a person can step through.

For one stupid, hopeful minute he thought of simply sealing it. Gin's book had a page on that too, and Rei made himself turn to it. Sealing a thin spot. Major operation. The veil compensates. Another location in the city thins. Underneath, in Gin's smaller hand, The Architect does not punish. It corrects. Seal the danger you know and you make one you don't. That was the rule the whole registered world worked under, and the Healer had built its plan inside it. Nobody could close Kita by force without opening somewhere else. It could only be held the slow way, by people. And the Healer had spent a month making the people grateful.

He sat back on his heels in the lamplight and let himself feel the elegance of it, because he had to understand the thing to fight it, and he could not understand it from a safe distance. It was beautiful. It was the most patient cruelty he had ever been close to. No grade in the city would ever point to a crime, because there was no crime. There was only kindness, handed out and adding up, until on the right night, with the dead already moving and every ward looking outward at the obvious monster, the curtain over Kita would lift on its own. Then something with grateful hands would climb to the one chair tall enough for what it wanted. It would call that finishing what death interrupted. Rei, if he let himself, would call it the end of the difference between the living city and the other side.

blocks.cap: What the thinning costs the people who still live there

blocks.p: He went up to Kita in the worst of the afternoon, when the heat sat on the rooftops like a second sky, and he made himself look at the people the plan treated as the inside of the cylinder. A woman watered morning glories on a balcony above a shuttered ramen counter. Children chalked a hopscotch grid on concrete that had not been right since 2011, concrete everyone stepped across without naming. An old man set a small dish of water on a windowsill for a wife the official records had closed years ago. None of them knew they lived at the seam. None of them had chosen to be the place where a demon decided the wall was already weak enough to be worth finishing.

He could feel it on them. Not as sight. He kept that shut. He felt it the way a joint feels a storm coming. They were tired here in a way the rest of Tokyo was not. They slept badly and blamed the heat. They lost small things and found them in places they swore they had already looked. A neighbourhood does not notice a curtain thinning over a month. It notices that the dead feel closer at Obon than they used to. It lights its lanterns a little earlier, and it tells itself it is only being devout. The Healer had not just chosen a weak wall. It had chosen people already half-trained by their own grief to mistake a door opening for the comfort of being remembered.
He stopped at the old man's window without meaning to, and that was when he saw the rats.

There were rats in the gutter under the sill, which meant nothing in August. Then he counted them, because Gin had once told him to, across the kitchen table, in a voice so dry that Rei had laughed. Count the rats. Twelve. Twelve rats in a gutter, and every one of them still, and every one of them turned the same way, toward the chalk grid where the concrete was wrong. They did not twitch or wash or quarrel. They watched. Rei felt his skin go cold in the heat.

He knew the page by heart now, because he had read it twice on the train. A cluster of twelve rats all looking at the same corner means something is wearing them, and has been for a while. The Demon does not need to follow Rei through Kita if the rats already do. Gin had written his name into the warning a year before any of this, and Rei had read it as a joke. A Class B entity, or a Master, could split a sliver of itself into the small animals of a district and ride their senses. Nobody looks at rats. A salt line would not stop it, because nothing was crossing. Something was only watching. The book said the right answer was to change districts. Rei could not change districts. Kita was the whole point. So he did the next thing the book allowed. He changed what he was doing. He walked on as if the window meant nothing to him, a tired young man in a tired street, and he did not look back at the gutter.

At the corner a woman stood with a brown dog on a lead, apologising to no one in particular. The dog had fixed on the hopscotch grid with its ears forward and a growl in its chest that never became a bark. Then, while Rei watched, it stopped. It backed away from the chalk with its tail down and went quiet, and pressed itself against the woman's shins. "He's been like this all week," she said. "It's the heat." Rei thanked her and kept walking. Gin's book had a line for that too. A dog that stops indicating and backs away is not saying the presence has gone. It is saying the presence is something it will not contest. It was the most important thing a dog could tell anyone, and the dog had been telling this street for a week.

He went back past the old man's window on the far pavement. The dish of water was trembling very faintly, with no wind to move it. The old man did not see it, because he was looking at the photograph beside it and not at the water. And Rei thought, this is the leash the Healer has on the whole district. Every one of them wants the wall thin. Every one of them, asked plainly, would say yes to one more night with the person the dish is for. The plan did not need to deceive Kita. It only needed to give a grieving city exactly what it had been praying for, on the one night the prayer was loudest, and let the answered prayer be the thing that broke the world.

blocks.break: A roof in Kita, at dusk

blocks.p: The Grid runner met him on the roof of a coin laundry at dusk. She was a narrow woman with a cloth bundle under her arm and the look of someone who had slept in her clothes, and she did not give a name. Someone had passed Rei to her, and that was enough. She unwrapped the bundle as if something inside it were alive. It was a mirror, square, dark-backed, longer on its shortest side than Rei's forearm.

"Three days," she said, before he could ask. "Three days feeding the same crow out of my hand, so it decides you are interesting and not a threat. Then the rite, at dawn or dusk, because the half-light is the condition. Not the ceremony. The light." She showed him the back of the frame, where a strip of seal paper was tucked under the edge. On it was one character, 視, sight, written in dried brown. "My own blood. The ink for the rest is charcoal and graveyard earth in water. Three black cords, each as long as your forearm. You lay the mirror face up and the paper face down on the glass, and you put food the crow already trusts at the edge. It has to land on the mirror. Not near it. On it. Then you draw the three cords across the glass from edge to edge without touching a feather, and you say the binding quietly. If it takes, the mirror shows you what the crow sees for one second. That second is the bond closing."
"How long does it last?"

"Until the crow dies or the mirror breaks. Whichever is first." She shrugged. "A mirror that outlives its crow goes dark and never binds again. It costs you a little to look, maybe a point of yourself for every ten minutes you hold it. Hold it longer than an hour and the bird starts sitting in your head. Do not do that." She held the mirror flat between them, and a crow lifted off the water tank behind her and went out over the roofs toward the river.
Rei looked down into the glass, and the city fell away under him.

He saw Kita from a height no person stands at. Tiled roofs, the river, the rail cut, the tiny lit squares of konbini. And over the place he had walked that afternoon he saw what his own eyes had never let him see at ground level. The membrane, drawn at last to its true scale. It lay over the ward like the skin over a knuckle when the fist is made, tight and shining and too thin. There was a darker crease in it where the chalk grid was. Around the crease the whole surface leaned, very slightly, the way water leans toward a drain.
Then something under the crease looked up.

Rei did not see it so much as feel the attention arrive, flat and enormous, through the crow and the glass and into his face. The runner slapped the mirror face down on the roof before he had finished flinching. "No," she said. "When a big one looks up at the bird, you are looking straight into what it sees of you. Face down. Always face down. The crow doesn't know to avoid them. Crows don't avoid anything." She wrapped the mirror in its cloth again, carefully, the way a person wraps something that breathes.

"The Division has a room of these," she said, and her mouth went thin. "Under the grey block at Ōji. The Mirror Room." Rei had heard the name from Okada, rows of mirrors to the ceiling, each one a slice of the city from a height no person stands at. He had never asked what the mirrors were. "A wall of crows," the runner said. "Every one fed by hand for three days, every one bound in blood. The people in there drink tea and watch birds' eyes." She tucked the bundle under her arm. "They taught the birds to see for them because they can't see into this place themselves. Ask yourself what that makes them."
"How do I get out from under the rats?" Rei asked. He had not meant to ask it aloud.

She looked at him with something close to pity. "You don't stop them. Salt does nothing. They aren't crossing, they're watching. You change the district you're working in." She hesitated. "Or you give them something else to watch. A toad. A big one, Bufo japonicus, the Grid keeps a rotation of them. You sit it in a sealed clay dish of graveyard earth. You write 替 on seal paper in graveyard-earth ink, substitution, and you bind the paper under the dish with red cord. Three drops of your own blood down the centre of its back, well clear of the glands at the sides. Then you push your signature out of yourself and into the animal. Fifteen, twenty-five minutes. When it takes, the toad swells and goes still, and to anything hunting you by your signature, the toad reads as you. You read as nothing."
"How long?"

"Two to four hours. Six with the earth under it. After that it dies, whatever you do. You can reverse it before then and it lives, and that's why the Grid keeps a rotation." She shook her head. "Not you, though. Not yet. You need symbol work at the second level and one of the body paths at the first, Psychokinesis or Psychometabolism. Ink alone won't push it. The body has to help." She looked away over the roofs. "I've done it more than once. I count them."
Then she went down the fire stairs, and Rei stayed on the roof until the last of the light went, feeling the place where the attention had touched him.

blocks.cap: The Healer's timetable, and why Obon was always the lock

blocks.p: Back in the heat-sick dark he finally understood the timing, and it landed like a key turning in a lock he had not known he was standing inside. It had to be Obon. Not as decoration, not as a pretty occasion for a haunting. As mechanism. Obon is the one stretch of the year when the dead are already moving toward the living, when the membrane works under its greatest load and holds against the strongest pull it ever faces. A wall is easiest to finish thinning when something is already leaning on it from the other side. The Healer had not weakened Kita and then waited for a convenient night. It had weakened Kita to the exact thinness at which the pull of Obon would do the last of the work for free, while every ward in the city read the rising pressure as nothing but the season.

So the trap had a clock now, and the clock was the festival itself. On the first night the families had floated the welcoming lanterns. Across the nights that followed the dead came, and stayed, and were fed and remembered. And on the final night, the night of okuribi, the sending-fire, when the rest of Tokyo lit its farewell and guided the dead gently back, the pull would reverse. The whole season's lean would swing the other way. At that hinge of the year, with the curtain at its thinnest and the city's attention turned to its own tender goodbye, the gap over the wound would stand open in both directions at once. The Healer had not chosen a night. It had chosen the single hour in the calendar when the door swings, and it had made its whole patient month a way of standing at that door when it did.

Rei wrote the hour down. He wrote it small, in the back of Gin's book, in the space Gin had left, the way Gin had taught him to write the things the records must never see. His hand did not shake until the pen was down. Three nights. Then the sending-fire, and the hinge, and the chair. Everything he did from here would happen inside that window, and the window was not his to widen. Whatever he meant to do about the trap, about his brother, about the factions all staring at the wrong demon, he would have to do inside three nights. He could not spend a fourth, because there would not be one. The festival that guides the dead home was also, this year, the lock the Healer had chosen, and it was already half turned.
